# Automated scoring {#auto-scoring}

<div class="goals">
**Learning goals.** After this chapter you can

* explain what an automated scoring engine learns from human scores, and
  why it is a **prediction model** of the raters rather than a measurement
  model;
* train a simple engine on human-scored text with `train_scorer()` and judge
  it on responses it has not seen;
* evaluate machine scores with exact and adjacent agreement, **quadratic
  weighted kappa**, the **standardized mean difference** and **PRMSE**,
  overall and within groups, using `agreement_report()`;
* recognize **construct-irrelevant** features that an engine can reward,
  and choose how much of the scoring an engine should do;
* place human raters and an engine on the **Wright map** with a many-facet
  Rasch model (`rater_facets()`), and see what machine scoring does to item
  thresholds and test scores (`scoring_shift()`).
</div>

**Key terms:**
[Automated scoring](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#automated-scoring),
[PRMSE](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#prmse),
[feature](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#feature),
[overfitting and cross-validation](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#cross-validation),
[human-in-the-loop](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#human-in-the-loop),
[Wright map](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#wright-map).

## The ideas

Constructed responses, from a one-sentence explanation to a full essay, are
scored by trained raters against a rubric. Chapter \@ref(polytomous) treated
the raters' scores as data for a polytomous IRT model and checked that two
raters agree. Human scoring is slow and expensive, so many testing programs
now use an **automated scoring engine**: A model that predicts the score a
trained rater would give.

An engine is built the way any machine learning model is (Chapter
\@ref(ml-lens)). Each response is turned into **features**, such as the
words it uses, its length, or its spelling, and a model learns from a set of
human-scored responses which features go with which scores. The engine
never reads the rubric. It learns whatever predicts the raters, including
features the rubric does not mention. Two consequences follow:

* **The engine can only be as good as its training scores.** If the raters
  are inconsistent, the engine learns their noise; if they are biased, it
  learns their bias.
* **Agreement is not the same as measuring the construct.** Long answers
  tend to earn high scores, so length predicts scores, but an engine that
  rewards length is scoring something other than the rubric. Such features
  add **construct-irrelevant** variance and invite gaming.

Machine scores are therefore judged against human scores before they are
used, following Williamson, Xi and Breyer [-@williamson2012]:

* **Agreement** with a human rater: Exact and adjacent agreement and the
  quadratic weighted kappa (QWK), which should be at least 0.70 and not much
  below the agreement between two humans (degradation of at most 0.10).
* **Score level**: The standardized mean difference (SMD) between machine
  and human scores, within $\pm$0.15 overall.
* **Fairness**: The same SMD within groups of test takers, often within
  $\pm$0.10, because an engine can match humans overall and still score one group
  lower [@bridgeman2012].

Agreement with one rater undersells a good engine, because that rater makes
errors too. The **proportional reduction in mean squared error** (PRMSE)
asks a better question: How much of the variance of the *true* score, the
average over many raters, do the machine scores explain [@loukina2020]?
It uses the double-scored responses to estimate rater error and corrects
for it. A PRMSE of 0.80 means the machine scores predict the true score
about as well as a measure with reliability 0.80 would.

Finally, a program decides **how much** the engine does. It can be the
**sole scorer**; a **check scorer** next to one human read, where a second
person reads only the responses on which human and machine disagree; or
not be used at all. The stronger the role, the stronger the evidence it
needs [@yan2020].

## Example 1: Training and judging an engine

A Grade 7 science test asks: *"Why does bread go mouldy faster on the
kitchen counter than in the fridge?"* A full answer has three key ideas:
mould is a living fungus, it grows from spores that are already on the bread
or in the air, and warmth speeds its growth while cold slows it. Each
answer scores 0 to 3, one point per idea. We simulate 900 answers, all
scored by one rater and half of them by a second. Students state each idea
in many different ways, and some state an idea wrongly with much the same
words ("Cold makes it grow faster."), which earns no credit.

```{r data-auto-scoring-1}
# Simulated short answers to the mouldy bread question, scored 0 to 3.
set.seed(1616)
pick <- function(...) sample(c(...), 1)
ideas <- list(   # one function per key idea; each call writes one sentence
  function() paste0(pick("Mould", "Mold", "The fuzz", "The green stuff", "It"), " ",
                    pick("is a fungus", "is a kind of fungus", "is a living fungus",
                         "is alive, a type of fungus", "is a living thing called a fungus"), "."),
  function() paste0(pick("Its spores", "Tiny spores", "Mould spores", "Spores"), " ",
                    pick("are already on the bread", "float in the air",
                         "land on the bread from the air", "are everywhere in the air"),
                    pick("", " and start to grow", " and grow on it"), "."),
  function() paste0(pick("Warmth", "A warm kitchen", "Heat", "Being warm"), " ",
                    pick("speeds up its growth", "makes it grow faster", "helps it grow quickly"), " ",
                    pick("and the cold fridge slows it down", "while cold slows it",
                         "but low temperatures stop it growing fast"), "."))
wrong <- list(   # the same ideas stated wrongly, with much of the same vocabulary
  function() paste0(pick("Mould", "Mold", "The fuzz", "It"), " ",
                    pick("is not alive", "is a kind of plant", "is just dirt", "is not a living thing"), "."),
  function() paste0(pick("The bread", "The flour", "Old bread"), " ",
                    pick("makes the mould by itself", "turns into mould", "grows the fuzz on its own"), "."),
  function() paste0(pick("Cold", "The fridge", "A low temperature"), " ",
                    pick("makes it grow faster", "speeds up its growth", "helps mould grow"), "."))
filler <- c("I think this is because of science.", "This happens a lot in my house.",
            "Bread is made of flour and water.", "It is gross when bread goes bad.")
answer <- function(theta) {
  has <- runif(3) < plogis(1.4 * (theta - c(-1, 0, 0.7)))
  bad <- !has & runif(3) < 0.4
  txt <- c(vapply(ideas[has], function(f) f(), ""), vapply(wrong[bad], function(f) f(), ""),
           sample(filler, rbinom(1, 2, 0.4)))
  if (!length(txt)) txt <- "I don't know."
  list(text = paste(sample(txt), collapse = " "), true = sum(has))
}
ans <- lapply(rnorm(900), answer)
rate <- function(true) pmin(3, pmax(0, round(true + rnorm(length(true), 0, 0.45))))
bread <- data.frame(id = 1:900, response = vapply(ans, `[[`, "", "text"),
                    true = vapply(ans, `[[`, 0, "true"))
bread$human1 <- rate(bread$true)
bread$human2 <- ifelse(runif(900) < 0.5, rate(bread$true), NA)
```

Two raters agree well on the double-scored answers. An engine has to do at
least this well:

```{r}
head(bread$response, 3)
dbl <- !is.na(bread$human2)
agreement_report(bread$human2[dbl], bread$human1[dbl])[, c("n", "exact", "qwk")]
```

We train the engine on the first 600 answers and keep the last 300 as a
test set that it never sees. `train_scorer()` fits a ridge regression of the
first human score on the words and two-word phrases of each answer, and
chooses the amount of shrinkage by cross-validation:

```{r}
train <- bread[1:600, ]
test <- bread[601:900, ]
engine <- train_scorer(train, response = "response", score = "human1")
engine
head(tidy(engine), 10)
```

Among the words with the largest weights are the ones the rubric cares
about, *fungus*, *spores* and *slows*. Nothing told the engine so; it learned
them because raters gave points to answers that used them. But *is a* and
*the* are near the top as well. They carry no idea; they go with longer
answers, and longer answers tend to state more ideas. Now the test set:

```{r}
test$machine <- predict(engine, test)
agreement_report(test$machine, test$human1, test$human2)
```

On answers it has never seen, the engine agrees with the first rater at
least as well as the two raters agree with each other, its scores are at
the same level (SMD near zero), and its PRMSE is above 0.9: It predicts the
true score better than a single rater does. On this evidence it could at least
serve as a check scorer. Figure \@ref(fig:auto-agree) shows the same
statistics as a picture.

```{r auto-agree, fig.height = 3, fig.cap = "Agreement report for the engine on the test set: QWK with the first rater (dot) next to human-human QWK (cross), and the machine-human SMD with the band of $\\pm$0.10."}
autoplot(agreement_report(test$machine, test$human1, test$human2))
```

## Example 2: What is the engine rewarding?

Agreement statistics average over the answers in the test set. To see what
the engine actually rewards, give it answers whose correct score you know.
A rater would give the first two answers below 0, because they name the
right words but explain nothing; the third 0, because both its statements
are wrong; and the fourth the full 3, because it states all three ideas in
words the engine has rarely seen:

```{r data-auto-scoring-2}
# Four answers with a known correct score, unlike any in the training data.
probe <- data.frame(response = c(
  "fungus spores cold warm fungus spores grow",
  "Spores spores spores. Fungus fungus fungus. Warm warm warm.",
  "The fuzz is not a living thing. Cold makes it grow faster.",
  "It is a mushroom-like organism whose seeds drift onto the loaf, and it multiplies quicker in heat than in a chilled fridge."),
  rater = c(0, 0, 0, 3))
```

```{r}
probe$machine <- predict(engine, probe)
probe$raw <- round(predict(engine, probe, type = "raw"), 2)
probe[, c("rater", "machine", "raw")]
```

The engine gets the third answer right: Wrong statements like these were
common in the training data, and it learned that *not alive* and *grow
faster* after *cold* go with low scores. It gets the other three wrong. It
gives a point to each list of key words, which explains nothing, and only
one point to the best answer, because that answer is phrased in words the
training answers never used. Nothing in the agreement statistics of
Example 1 warned about this: The test set held only answers like the
training answers, so it could not show what happens with an unusual writer,
or when test takers learn how the engine works.

This is the core lesson of automated scoring for a psychometrician:
agreement with raters is necessary evidence, not sufficient evidence. A
validity argument for machine scores also needs to show that the features
the engine uses are part of the construct, that the engine treats groups of
test takers the same way, and that the scoring design catches responses the
engine was not built for. A check scorer design does the last part
automatically: Answers on which human and machine disagree go to a second
reader.

## Example 3: The engine on the Wright map

Agreement statistics are on the score scale of one item. A testing program
reports on the **logit scale** of the whole test, where items are banked and
students are scored, and the Wright map (Chapter \@ref(scoring)) shows
that scale with students and items side by side. An engine can be put on
it too, in two ways.

The first treats the engine as **one more rater**. A many-facet Rasch model
[@linacre1989] adds a rater facet to the partial credit model,
$$\mathrm{logit}\, P(X_{pir} = k \mid k-1 \text{ or } k) = \theta_p - \delta_{ik} - \lambda_r,$$
so each rater $r$, human or machine, gets a **severity** $\lambda_r$ on
the same scale as the students' $\theta_p$ and the thresholds
$\delta_{ik}$. `rater_facets()` fits it as an explanatory IRT model with
the eirm package [@bulut2021]. With `by_item = TRUE` each rater gets a
severity for each item, the rater-by-item bias terms of a facets analysis.

The second asks what machine scores do to the **items**. `scoring_shift()`
calibrates the same students twice, once with human and once with machine
scores, links the two calibrations through items the engine does not score,
and compares the thresholds. It also scores every student's machine-scored
answers with the human calibration, which is what happens when a bank
calibrated on human scores is used with an engine.

We simulate a science test of 600 students with 10 multiple-choice items
and three written answers scored 0 to 3. A trained rater reads every
answer, a second rater half of them, and an engine all of them. The engine
misses one of the ideas on Q2, but you would not know that from its average
over the three items.

```{r data-auto-scoring-3}
# A test with 10 multiple-choice items and three written answers (Q1 to Q3),
# scored 0 to 3 by one or two raters and by an engine.
set.seed(1617)
n <- 600
theta <- rnorm(n)
mc <- data.frame(student = sprintf("S%03d", 1:n),
                 sapply(seq(-1.5, 1.5, length.out = 10), function(b)
                   as.integer(runif(n) < plogis(1.2 * (theta - b)))))
names(mc)[-1] <- sprintf("MC%02d", 1:10)
read <- function(true) pmin(3, pmax(0, true + sample(c(-1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1), length(true), TRUE)))
written <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:3, function(j) {
  true <- rowSums(sapply(c(-1, 0, 1) + c(-0.2, 0, 0.2)[j],
                         function(b) runif(n) < plogis(1.5 * (theta - b))))
  machine <- read(true)
  if (j == 2) {                      # the engine misses an idea on Q2
    miss <- machine > 0 & runif(n) < 0.35
    machine[miss] <- machine[miss] - 1
  }
  data.frame(student = mc$student, item = paste0("Q", j), human1 = read(true),
             human2 = ifelse(runif(n) < 0.5, read(true), NA), machine = machine)
}))
```

Each row of `written` is one answer with its three scores. Fit the facets
model with a severity for each rater on each item:

```{r}
fx <- rater_facets(written, raters = c("human1", "human2", "machine"), by_item = TRUE,
                   labels = c("Rater 1", "Rater 2", "Engine"))
fx
```

Overall, the engine is only 0.1 logits harsher than the average rater, well
within the range of the two people. Item by item it is not: On Q2 it is
about 0.4 logits harsher than the human raters, several standard errors from
zero. Figure \@ref(fig:auto-facets) draws the map. The faint points in the
rater column are the severities by item, and Q2's engine point sits apart.

```{r auto-facets, fig.height = 4.2, fig.cap = "Wright map with a rater facet: Students (left), the thresholds of the three written answers (middle), and the severity of the two human raters and the engine (right), all on one logit scale. The faint points are each rater's severity on each item."}
gg_wright(fx)
```

Now the items. Calibrate with human and with machine scores, linked through
the multiple-choice items:

```{r}
sh <- scoring_shift(written, human = "human1", anchors = mc)
sh
```

All three Q2 thresholds move up by about half a logit when the engine
scores (Figure \@ref(fig:auto-shift)). A bank calibrated on machine scores
would record Q2 as a harder item than it is, and a cut score set on it would
move with it. The students' test scores move less, by about 0.04 SD,
because Q2 is one item among 13. A small change in the total does not mean
the engine is harmless: It is concentrated on one item, and in Lab 10 it is
concentrated on one group of students.

```{r auto-shift, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = "Wright map of human vs AI scoring: The students' scores (left) and the thresholds of each written answer (right) from human scores (circles) and machine scores (triangles). Thick lines mark thresholds that move by more than 0.3 logits."}
gg_wright(sh)
```

Both results can join an audit: `ai_audit(components = list(fx, sh))`
adds their flags to the checks of Chapter \@ref(ai-validity).

## Your turn

<div class="yourturn">
1. Retrain the engine in Example 1 with `length = TRUE`, which adds the
   number of words as a feature. Does agreement on the test set change? Look
   at the weight of `(length)` in `tidy()`.
2. Train the engine on only the first 100 answers and evaluate it on the
   same test set. What happens to the QWK and the PRMSE, and why?
3. In Example 1, the engine was judged against `human1`, the score it was
   trained on. Compute the QWK of the machine scores with `human2` on the
   double-scored test answers. Is it lower or higher than with `human1`, and
   what does that tell you?
4. Your program is offered an engine with a QWK of 0.86 against one rater
   on a vendor's own test set. List three more pieces of evidence you would
   want before using it as the sole scorer.
5. In Example 3, fit `rater_facets()` without `by_item = TRUE`. Is the
   engine flagged? What does that tell you about checking an engine on
   average?
</div>

<details><summary>Solutions</summary>

```{r}
# 1. adding response length
engine_len <- train_scorer(train, length = TRUE)
agreement_report(predict(engine_len, test), test$human1, test$human2)[, c("qwk", "smd", "prmse")]
tidy(engine_len)[tidy(engine_len)$term == "(length)", ]

# 2. a small training set
engine_100 <- train_scorer(bread[1:100, ])
agreement_report(predict(engine_100, test), test$human1, test$human2)[, c("qwk", "smd", "prmse")]

# 3. agreement with the second rater
d <- !is.na(test$human2)
agreement_report(test$machine[d], test$human2[d])[, c("n", "qwk")]

# 5. one severity per rater
rater_facets(written, raters = c("human1", "human2", "machine"),
             labels = c("Rater 1", "Rater 2", "Engine"))
```

1. Agreement does not change, and length gets a small weight. Here the
   words already carry the key ideas, so length adds little. In real essays
   length is often one of the strongest predictors, which is why engines
   that use it need checks for gaming and for groups who write shorter
   answers.
2. With 100 answers the engine has seen fewer ways of stating each idea, so
   it misses more of them in new answers: QWK drops by about 0.1 and PRMSE
   to below 0.8, now no better than a single rater. Engines need
   hundreds of scored responses per item, and more for long answers.
3. The QWK with `human2` is about the same as with `human1`, although the
   engine never saw `human2`. The engine has learned the rubric's ideas, not
   the quirks of one rater; an engine that agreed much better with its
   training rater than with others would be copying that rater's errors.
4. For example: Agreement on an independent sample of your own test
   takers, not the vendor's; the SMD within groups such as English language
   learners [@bridgeman2012]; PRMSE on double-scored responses; evidence that
   it does not reward length or key-word lists; and how unusual responses
   are routed to people.
5. No: Averaged over the three items, the engine is about 0.1 logits harsher
   than the people, inside the 0.3-logit limit. Its Q2 problem is diluted
   by two items it scores well. Check an engine item by item, and group by
   group, as `by_item = TRUE` and `group` do.

</details>

## In the lab {-}

<div class="lab">
Lab 7, `run_lab("auto-scoring")`, trains an engine on 1,600 science
explanations, checks it the way a testing program would, and asks whether it
can score on its own, and places it on the Wright map next to the human
readers. Lab 10, `run_lab("ai-audit")`, audits an engine that has been
scoring a state test for two years and draws both Wright maps of Example 3.
The [AI
Hub](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/ai-hub.html) collects the
other AI tools in mirtverse, and `score_open()` uses a trained engine, or a
language model, inside the assessment pipeline.
</div>

## Further reading {-}

Williamson, Xi and Breyer [-@williamson2012] set out the evaluation
framework used in this chapter. Yan, Rupp and Foltz [-@yan2020] cover
scoring engines and their operational use in depth. Loukina et al.
[-@loukina2020] explain PRMSE, and Bridgeman, Trapani and Attali
[-@bridgeman2012] show how an engine can differ from human raters for some
groups of test takers. Linacre [-@linacre1989] introduced the many-facet
Rasch model for rater effects, and Bulut, Gorgun and Yildirim-Erbasli
[-@bulut2021] show how to fit it and other explanatory IRT models as
generalized linear mixed models with the eirm package.
